Students that reflected on the reasons for the differing perspectives amongst nationalist thinkers in their evaluation were typically rewarded at higher levels.
71523-jun24-c-06:
This was the most popular section C question. Most students were able to identify that equality for women was the aim for all feminists. Students that approached the question by considering the different strands of feminism and their critique of the position of women legally, economically socially often did well. This was particularly true when answers were developed by discussing why there was disagreement between the different strands. Students were able to cite a good range of thinkers with Millet, bell hooks, De Beauvoir, Rowbotham and Gillman all being accurately used in strong responses. As with all the

section C responses there was a tendency for many answers to present a list of key thinkers’ ideas, sometimes returning to the focus of the question at the end of each paragraph. Whilst these answers often had much creditworthy material they did not address the thrust of the question as well as responses that dealt with the question thematically using thinkers as examples.
71523-jun24-c-07: This question was done by a very small number of students. Most of the responses were at mid and lower-levels and did not address the key thinkers with confidence, if they were mentioned at all.
71523-jun24-c-08: This question was popular, with a higher proportion of students attempting it than in previous series. Most students were able to identify that it focused on a tension within anarchism between syndicalists such Proudhon and egoists such as Stirner. Students who cited other libertarian thinkers were credited, such a Rothbard, and received higher levels if this was in addition to discussion of key thinkers. However, where students only relied on the ideas of thinkers that were outside the specification they were limited to level 2 as per the rubric in the mark scheme. Responses that scored highly were able to challenge the premise of the question suggesting that the main motivation of anarchism was to end oppression at the hands of the state. As with all the section C responses there was a tendency for many answers to present a list of key thinkers’ ideas, sometimes returning to the focus of the question at the end of each paragraph. Whilst these answers often had much creditworthy material, they did not address the thrust of the question as well as responses that dealt with the question thematically using thinkers as examples.
71523-jun24-c-09: Most students were able to identify that the often the tension between light and dark green ecologists is about the status human beings morally and economically in relation to other living creatures and the natural environment. Students who reflected on concepts such as anthropocentrism, the Gaia hypothesis, and sustainability were given credit this was often enhanced when this was linked accurately to key thinkers. As with all the section C responses there was a tendency for many answers to present a list of key thinkers’ ideas, sometimes returning to the focus of the question at the end of each paragraph. Whilst these answers often had much creditworthy material, they did not address the thrust of the question as well as responses that dealt with the question thematically using thinkers as examples.
71523-jun25-a-01: Most students were able to identify that revolution was method to achieve the aims of socialism. Students that did well were often able to make a clear distinction between Luxemburg and Marx, though less successful responses tended to repeat the similarities between them, that a revolution was required to completely eradicate capitalism as an economic system. Students who scored high marks often also developed the ideas of Webb (evolutionary socialism), Crossland (Social Democracy) and Giddens (the Third Way) well. Answers that scored less well tended repetitively focus on the need for equality rather than the method of achieving it.
71523-jun25-a-02: This question was generally done less well than question 1. Answers that scored in the highest level had a clear understanding of capitalism as an economic system. Answers at middle or lower levels of response, either did not demonstrate a clear grasp of what capitalism was or tended to repeat that liberals liked capitalism without nuance. For those students chose to write about Mill and Locke, there was a tendency to repeat arguments about laissez-faire economics. A common feature of the less successful responses was that students suggested that liberals were anti-capitalist.
71523-jun25-a-03:
This question was least successfully answered in general, in section A. The responses that scored well often referred to a range of thinkers’ ideas on private property such as Nozick and Rand (and the idea that private property is a freedom to be preserved) Burke (as source social order and continuity) Oakeshott (that a pragmatic empirical approach should by the state towards private property that could enhance social cohesion) and Hobbes (that private property is inherently insecure in the state of nature). Students at middle and lower levels either repeated the ideas of Nozick and Rand. Explanations of Hobbes ideas on property were

often inaccurate at middle and lower levels or tended to simply assert that all conservatives favoured private property without nuance.
71523-jun25-ex-04:
Most students identified that Nozick believed that society was a collection of individuals and that Burke considered it to be comprised of “little platoons.” Responses at higher level discussed provenance in a meaningful way, recognising one as a Guardian obituary (more reflective, less theoretical), the other from a conservative website. Responses that scored well also used the extracts as a springboard, referring to key ideas of Nozick and Burke beyond the text as well as other thinkers, such as Rand’s atomism. This question has 3 command words; Analyse Evaluate and Compare, the final one of which is often a feature of the highest scoring answers. Answers at middle levels often compare in an implicit fashion, giving 2 parallel accounts of the extracts. Less successful answers had misconceptions, such as mistaking Nozick for a liberal, neglecting to situate him within the New Right, or simply paraphrased the extracts without providing significant analysis or evaluation of their own.

Section C The familiar pattern of a very high proportion of students answering the Feminism Nationalism and Anarchism essays, with far fewer Ecologism and Multiculturalism responses, continued this year. The best answers in general focused on the key debate in the question, rather than giving a narrative account of the ideas of the thinkers (although this was still credited at middle or lower levels, depending on the quality of the discussion). Evaluations at higher levels often made a clear judgement on the proposition (it did not matter whether it agreed with the statement or not), and gave clear reasons for that judgement, answers at middle levels tended to summarise arguments made.
71523-jun25-c-05: Students who scored highly analysed whether self-determination was a shared goal or not, then explored different justifications across cultural, civic, and expansionist nationalisms. Student who scored at lower levels often misunderstood the question, focusing on whether each thinker had some principles, rather than whether the thinkers had principles in common.
71523-jun25-c-06: Most students were able to identify that liberal feminist tended to focus on legal equality in society whereas radical feminists were concerned with ending patriarchy in all aspects of life, including in the home. Students who argued that whilst legal equality is always necessary, it is not always sufficient to achieve the goals of feminism. Answers at lower and middle levels, tended to give narrative accounts of the ideas of key thinkers (to varying degrees of accuracy) without evaluating the extent to which gender distinctions should be removed.
71523-jun25-c-07: This question was done by a very small number of students. The quality of answers was better this year with some responses reaching higher levels. Those that did score well typically addressed a range of thinkers focusing on the tensions between individual liberty and tolerance, citing thinkers such as Berlin, and recognition of groups, citing thinkers such as Kymlicka.
71523-jun25-c-08: Most students were able to identify some thinkers thought violence was essential to the removal of the state, citing thinkers such a Kropotkin. Students who cited other libertarian thinkers were credited, such a Rothbard, and received higher levels if this was in addition to discussion of key thinkers. However, as was the case last year, a small but significant number of students who only relied on the ideas of thinkers that were outside the specification were limited to level 2 as per the rubric in the mark scheme. Students who scored marks at lower and middle levels often misrepresented the attitude Stirner towards violence or wanted to try and argue that individualists’ thinkers all had one view, and the collectivists another. Students that scored the highest level evaluated the extent to which violence was a requirement of anarchism.
71523-jun25-c-09: This question was rarely successfully answered; however, those students who scored highly avoided a narrative account of the environmental of key thinkers and directly interrogated the potential contradiction between growth and ecological protection. Strong answers often cited Bookchin on capitalism, analysing the extent to which the pursuit of increased economic output will be detrimental to the environment. The least successful responses tended to give an account of ecological issues.
